fields.meta_title: Minimalist Landing Page: Examples and Builder | Emergent
fields.meta_description: See a minimalist landing page in four layouts, each with one action. Check text contrast and keep signups in a database you own. Free to start.
fields.h1: Build a Minimalist Landing Page With One Message and One Action
fields.hero_description: Build a minimalist landing page with one headline and one button, and save each signup to a database you own.
fields.features_heading: Fewer Parts, Each One Placed on Purpose
fields.features_subheading: A minimalist landing page carries one message and one action, and cuts every part that serves neither. Six parts hold it together.
fields.feature_1:
One headline and one button from a prompt

Describe the offer in a sentence and name the one action a visitor should take. Emergent builds the page around those two parts, and you move or remove anything later by prompting.
fields.feature_2:
Empty space treated as part of the layout

NN/g calls the empty areas of an interface negative space, also called white space. Ask for wide margins above and below the headline, and give the button room of its own.
fields.feature_3:
Pale colors checked against the 4.5:1 line

A light gray headline on white can look calm and still be hard to read. WCAG 2.2 asks for a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for text. Test each pair before you publish.
fields.feature_4:
No menu bar beside the one button

In Laws of UX's words, the time it takes to make a decision increases with the number and complexity of choices. Drop the nav menu and footer links, and leave one choice.
fields.feature_5:
Each entry saved to a table you own

Every entry from the page's one form lands in a database you own. Ask for the columns you need, such as email and project type, and Emergent builds that table with the page.
fields.feature_6:
Hosted on your domain, exported as code

Publish on your own domain; custom domains are included and use credits. On paid plans, export the full code to your GitHub repository and keep the page wherever you host it.

fields.tab_content_1:
A whole first screen for a $38 mug

Kelda Ceramics sells one stoneware mug, and its page shows nothing else. A full-width photo of the mug fills the first screen, with a short headline and a single Buy button laid over it. There is no menu. This week the page had 640 visitors and took 29 orders, each saved with the glaze the buyer picked.
fields.tab_content_2:
No images, and 17 quote requests this month

Osterlin Translation works from German and Dutch into English, and its page is set in type alone on an off-white background. A large headline names the service, a short paragraph explains it, and one button opens the request form. The page drew 17 quote requests this month, each saved with its language pair.
fields.tab_content_3:
A photo on the left, a 3-field form on the right

Fenmarch Studio designs house extensions. Its page splits the screen. A photo of one finished extension fills the left half; a headline and a form fill the right. The form asks for 3 fields: name, email, and project type. Nadia Varno's kitchen extension was the 14th inquiry this month, saved to the studio's database.
fields.tab_content_4:
An email is all it asks, and 1,204 people gave one

Quillary is a notes app that has not launched yet. Its page says what the app does in one sentence, then shows one email field and a Get early access button in the middle of the screen. Nothing sits below them but a one-line footer. So far 1,204 people have signed up, and each address is a row in a table the team owns.

fields.howto_title: How to Build a Minimalist Landing Page
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to a minimalist landing page that says one thing, asks for one action, and stays readable, then build it with Emergent.
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Set the type and one accent
fields.howto_step_1_des: Write the sentence a visitor should remember if they read nothing else, such as "Hand-thrown mugs, fired once a month." If it takes two sentences to say, the page is carrying two offers. Keep the stronger one and give the other a page of its own.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Decide the one thing a visitor does here: buy, book, request a quote, or leave an email. Laws of UX gives the advice to minimize choices when response times are critical to decrease decision time. Remove secondary links that point anywhere else.
fields.howto_step_3_des: List every part you planned, from a logo strip to testimonials to footer links. For each one, ask whether it backs up the message or helps the visitor act. Keep the parts that do and delete the rest, even the ones that took a day to make.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Pick one typeface in two weights, and keep one accent color for the button alone. Hold body lines to about 65 characters. WCAG's AAA guideline on visual presentation says width is no more than 80 characters. Treat 80 as the ceiling.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Describe the page in a prompt
fields.howto_step_5_des: Put the message, the action, the typeface, and the accent color into one prompt, with the fields the form needs. Emergent builds the page and the table behind its form. Prompt again to widen a margin or rename the button.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Check the first screen on a phone
fields.howto_step_6_des: Open the page on a phone and look at the first screen only: the headline and the button should both be there, with nothing pushing them down. Tap the button with your thumb, send a test entry, and find it in the table.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Publish and change one part a week
fields.howto_step_7_des: Publish the page and leave it alone for a week. Then change a single part, such as the headline or the button label, and compare the next week's entries with the last. Two changes at once leave you guessing which one worked.

faq_plan.q: What is a minimalist landing page?
faq_plan.a: A minimalist landing page is a single page built around one offer and one next step, with every other part taken out. NN/g describes minimalist design as an approach that seeks to simplify interfaces by removing unnecessary elements or content that does not support user tasks. On a landing page, that task is the one button or form.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a minimalist landing page?
faq_plan.a: Decide the sentence the page must say and the thing a visitor should do, then cut every part that serves neither. Describe those choices and your typeface to Emergent's AI landing page builder. It builds the page with a database for the entries, and you adjust spacing or copy by prompting again.

faq_plan.q: What should a minimalist landing page include?
faq_plan.a: A headline that states the offer, a line or two of support, one image or none, and one button or form. Add proof only where a visitor needs it to act, such as a price or a delivery time. On a page Emergent builds, that form saves each entry to a database you own.

faq_plan.q: Does a minimalist landing page work for people who scan a code on a poster?
faq_plan.a: Yes, as long as the headline repeats the poster's offer word for word. A visitor who scans a printed code arrives on a phone. Put the headline and the button on the first screen and leave out anything that needs scrolling. The qr code landing page guide covers the code itself and where to print it.

faq_plan.q: How much white space should a minimalist landing page have?
faq_plan.a: Enough that the headline and the button each read on their own at a glance. A practical start is to leave space above and below the headline at least as tall as the headline itself. Keep the same clearance around the button, then judge the result on a phone, where the screen is narrowest.

faq_plan.q: What colors work on a minimalist landing page?
faq_plan.a: Start with a neutral background, one text color, and one accent that only the button uses. Then check each pair against WCAG 2.2: large-scale text, such as a big headline, can pass at 3:1, while body copy needs 4.5:1 or more.

faq_plan.q: How do I keep a minimalist landing page readable on a phone?
faq_plan.a: Test it on a real phone, not a resized browser window. Body text should read without zooming, the headline should wrap without leaving one word alone on a line, and the button should be wide enough for a thumb. The mobile landing page guide covers phone layouts in more detail.

faq_plan.q: Do I need a template to build a minimalist landing page?
faq_plan.a: No. Emergent builds the page from a plain-English prompt and changes it by prompting. You start from your own message instead of someone else's sections. On paid plans, the full code exports to your GitHub repository, where you or a developer can edit it directly.

faq_plan.q: What fonts suit a minimalist landing page?
faq_plan.a: A serif or a sans serif both work, as long as the headline is set large and heavy and the body face stays clear at small sizes. NN/g notes that bold or large typography becomes another tool for communicating meaning when there are few elements on the page. To swap the face later, prompt Emergent with the new font name.

faq_plan.q: Can a minimalist landing page use motion?
faq_plan.a: Yes, if each motion is small and has a reason, such as a fade on the headline or a hover state on the button. Skip looping backgrounds, which put a second moving thing next to the one action. Pages built around motion are covered in the animated landing page guide.

plan.angle: The SERP for minimalist landing page is galleries, stock photos and Pinterest boards: they show clean layouts but never say how to choose the one message and the one action, what to cut, or how to keep a pale palette readable. This page shows four minimalist layouts (photo hero, type only, split screen, single email field), each with one action and its result counted, and gives the sourced rules that keep a sparse page usable: fewer choices (Hick's law), contrast of at least 4.5:1, a readable line length. Animated, interactive, modern and mobile landing pages are siblings and stay out of the headings.

findings.quote: A full-width photo of the mug fills the first screen, with a short headline and a single Buy button laid over it.
findings.issue: The tab is labelled Photo Hero and the copy describes a full-width photo with the headline and button laid over it. uc-1 shows no photo: a heading sits above a small product card with a cube icon and the Buy button inside the card. The layout is what this tab exists to show, so the image tells a different story. Same class in the same tab: mockup photoHero 'Fill the first screen with one full-width photo of the mug, lay a short headline and a single Buy button over it'; image_brief prompt 'Fill the first screen with one mug photo and a single Buy button'.
findings.fix: Redraw uc-1 so a full-width image area fills the panel with the headline and Buy button over it (or a clearly marked photo block above them). If the engine cannot draw a photo, rewrite tab 1 copy, label, mockup and chip to a layout the image actually shows.

findings.quote: Its page splits the screen. A photo of one finished extension fills the left half; a headline and a form fill the right.
findings.issue: uc-3 draws a single column: heading, three fields and a Send inquiry button. There is no photo and no split. Same class: tab_label_3 'Split Screen'; images.tab_image_3 alt 'Fenmarch Studio's split-screen page'; mockup splitScreen 'Put one photograph of a finished extension on the left. On the right, put a headline above a form'; image_brief prompt 'Put one project photo beside a 3-field inquiry form'.
findings.fix: Redraw uc-3 with the `columns` block: a photo panel on the left and the heading, 3 fields and button on the right, and keep the alt text in line with what is drawn.

findings.quote: A light gray headline on white can look calm and still be hard to read. WCAG 2.2 asks for a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for text.
findings.issue: The source (SC 1.4.3, Level AA) sets 4.5:1 with an exception: 'Large-scale text and images of large-scale text have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1'. Applied to a headline, the feature drops that scope (rework checklist 2) and contradicts faq 6 'large-scale text, such as a big headline, can pass at 3:1' (rework checklist 5). The H3 'Pale colors checked against the 4.5:1 line' carries the same unscoped number. No other field has it.
findings.fix: Keep the scope, for example: 'A light gray line on white can look calm and still be hard to read. WCAG 2.2 sets 4.5:1 for body text and 3:1 for large text. Test each pair before you publish.' Adjust the H3 if needed and keep the body in the 165-182 band.

findings.quote: WCAG's AAA guideline on visual presentation says width is no more than 80 characters.
findings.issue: SC 1.4.8 asks that 'a mechanism is available to achieve' a width of no more than 80 characters; the sentence leaves out that condition. The AAA label is kept and the step's advice is a recommendation, so this is a note.
findings.fix: Optionally: 'WCAG's AAA guideline on visual presentation lists a width of no more than 80 characters.'
